title: Joe Darensbourg and Minor "Ram" Hall Interview, 1957-04-18

pages.label: 001_Joe Darensbourg and Minor "Ram" Hall Interview, 1957-04-18 Part 1

blocks.x: Joe Derensburg with Mona Hall, April 18, 1957, Reel 1.
Yeah, man, I've been going fishing. I ain't had no luck last time. One time, my wife, I made a fish, man. You sure they want to cut nine catfish that long? Catfish?
Oh, no, not that long. Yeah. Oh, yeah. Here's Joe. And old catfish that big. Okay, here.
Look, wait a minute. New Iberia. All right. I'm going sadly. No, I'm just going to cut out. Look, I'm going sadly. Sadly, see. If I had no luck, I'll bring you out one more.
What you see? Bring it out to my house. Yeah, yeah. Because I want you to help me to do a little

little catfish. Yeah. I had to drive to my prison. You know, I had to do yoga fishing. You know, I said, you like fish like that? I said, I'm getting on the good side with it. And look, I had two catfish behind the box. It's called a Wednesday. And you know, I'm getting the stuff together, you know. I throw that all in a bag, you know. Oh, yeah? I said, I won't forget you. You know, you're just letting me roll up there the worst. Now, this guy, you know what? This guy can cook. You know, like you. He can really cook. That's a champion. You know what I mean? I made it last week. Chopped suede. I don't forget how to make that sweet and sour. This guy, you talking about cook. This guy is cool. How about you? Oh, I cook this guy. Now, you used to come to my house. Do you remember they making these things? Remember you made them red beans on the top? I got to go. You too, dude. All right, man. Yeah. Thank you very much. Take a picture with you. I'll show you guys before I go in the picture. No, it's not too long. It's all finished. It's all. I'll talk to you next week. Yeah, come back to me. I want him to come back here, you know. I'll call you before I go to New York. I'm going to hear what the union's going to do about the see what life he's going to make up now. Look, he's going to take something about our old-hand money. What if I got my hair on a guy, I'll get out of there. I'll get out of there. I'm quitting. I'm trying to stop a man from getting that little money. I'll be in there. Miss Hall told me, he know he's coming to Bells of Cab. He said, what kind of man is that? He said, we can't stop nothing like this. Yeah. Well, all right, Brian. Thanks. Thanks. I've been there. Thank you very much. I got to get home for this. All right. George, if you're a little. Yeah, if we go
crawfish next week, I'm going to. Yeah, I'm going to call by and have people

warning me about property. But I'm going to bring you this check. It's the last thing I do. I know I'm going to have a fight with Teddy because I used to get Teddy on a blue deal. No, you bring it by my house. Yeah, well, I'm going to say it if it
don't rain. Bring it by my house and then maybe you can give me some ideas about this

thing out there. Okay, yeah, because I got some nothing to do now, man. Yeah, and any repair out of my house, I do it myself. Okay. I'll call you and if necessary, I'll come pick you up. Okay. Yeah. Okay. All right. Thanks a lot. I will. Yes. All right. See you. Thank you. Thank you. Okay. Have a drink. Oh, Ram looks pretty good. Yeah. I thought, you know, like I need to pick this on. Looks so nice. Yeah. I want to close you. Where's my
matches? No, you always want something. Yeah, give me a little more tonic here. You got it.
Did you have my cup? Oh, that's fine. Give me that. Jim Beam. You think that'll be enough to carry it? I will. Look at that next door. What are you wearing that? The sky is
the limit. That's the way they pull this out in New Orleans. That's the one of them New Orleans drinks.
You want a little Coke? You want Coke? You want a drink there? Well, let's change it. I'll have

the drink there. All right. You can change it. Yeah, give me a little liquor and a glass and put some ice in my hand. That's good. Used to be a joint in New Orleans. Yeah. Used to sell wine a long time ago. And had these big tall glasses, but they'd fill these glasses with the crushed ice. First and then they'd pour the wine in there. Yeah. And they had some guy around in New Orleans. His name was Joe Mapu. Yeah. And Joe Mapu was supposed to be kind of dumb. But he used to come in the place one day and he says, hey man, he says, he says, give me a glass of wine there. He says, but I want the ice in my hand. Separate.
Ice in my hand. Yeah.

He wasn't dumb. Bartender gave him a glass full of ice and he says, no, you fill that glass up with wine like you suppose. No kidding. And Bartender, he was kind of dumbfounded, but he filled the glass up. And old Mapu took and drank half of this wine and then took the ice that he had and it filled the glass up again. He says, you see that? He says, you guys say, I'm dumb. He says, no, I still got a full glass.

I'm going to ask you a few questions about your younger days. All right. You know, like 50, 60 years ago. That's about right. That's about 55 years ago. When were you born? About 70 years ago? 1906. What 1906? Come on. Now you can tell, you know, we're old friends. You
don't act like. July, July. Who do you think you are? Edgar Allen? July the 9th, 1906. Yes. Where was that? In Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Yes. On 1440 North Boulevard
Street. Boulevard Street. Boulevard Street. Sounds funny to me. Boulevard Street. All right. How

was your story? Well, they got funny names in Baton Rouge, but you ought to know that anyway. So, uh, was there much, much music in Baton Rouge? They had a lot of music in Baton Rouge. When I was about 16 years old, I played in a band in Baton Rouge called, uh, Tuts Johnson's Band. Yeah. And
personally, I think that was one of the best bands ever to come out of Louisiana. Really? Yes. You
mean, you mean as good as a good New Orleans band? Better than a lot of those New Orleans bands. That
band used to go to New Orleans and cut a lot of those New Orleans bands. Buddy P.T. was the trumpet player in that band. Oh, yeah. You remember Buddy P.T.? Yeah. Yeah. So, what was he

doing with Baton Rouge? He came from New Orleans to work in this band. Oh, yeah? What? That must have been about, about 1922 or something? Just about. That's fine. What were you playing? What instruments? Clarinet. My teacher played in the band. When did you first become interested
in music? Oh, no, when I was a small kid. My ambition was to play on a circuit. Yeah. My first
instrument was a violin. Oh. The next was a piano. Did you study those instruments? Yeah. But
I had an uncle that used to play with the old Hagenbeck-Wallace circus. The trombone, played trombone. And every year when the circus came to town, I wanted to go with him. And, uh, he
used to tell me, he says, well, uh, he says, man, he says, you can't go with the circus or playing a violin or a piano. He says, you don't care of those kind of instruments. You've got
to play a brass horn or drums or, or some kind of reed instrument, like a clarinet. So, I

settled for the clarinet. And, uh, like I said, this teacher of mine, uh, Manuel Rock, played in this band, Tooth Johnson's band, that, uh, Buddy Petit was in. I started taking lessons from him when I was about, uh, four and eleven years old. On clarinet? Yeah. And when I was about twelve years old, he used to take me on some of those gigs. Uh-huh. Some of those dances, you know, things like that they played and let me sit in with them. Well, I mean, at
that time, was, was the kind of music they played about the same as in New Orleans? Same style?

Exactly the same, yeah. Exactly the same? Oh, yeah. That was really one of the good bands. What kind of places did you play with the band? They played lawn parties, dances, parades. Did they have parades in Baton Rouge? Oh, yeah. They had them funeral parades in Baton Rouge, just like they had in New Orleans. Oh, yeah. Did you hear them play any of them? Exactly. Sure. But the thing I can remember the best is when those bands used to ballyhoo would dance. Like,
they was going to have a dance at night, they would, they would be on one of those, uh, wagons,

you know? Was it, was it, uh, like a truck or with horses? Horses. Horses. Horses. Not, not, no, no truck, no. They had very few trucks in those days. No, and those cats would stop in front of every saloon. Yeah. And the saloon that'd give them the most drinks, they would play there the longest. They'd bring the drinks out or would they invite them? They'd bring them out. They'd bring them out? Sometimes they'd bring them out and sometimes the guys would have a little short intermission and go in and take a couple of shots and come back out and play. But they had exactly the same deal, that second line deal that they had in New Orleans. No, no different. Because I used to do the same thing in New Orleans. I took lessons from Piku. Did you? I didn't bother. Piku and my father was good friends. Oh. Was your father a musician? Yeah. Played a little E-flat cornet.
Was he a professional musician? No, no, no. He wasn't a professional musician.

Mostly as a hobby. They had a brass band among his friends. My father was a shoemaker. Mm-hmm. But they had a brass band among his friends. My father was from a little small town in Louisiana called Glen.
Did they speak French or Creole in the family? Oh, he, my father talked real French. He talked both, Creole and French. And probably English much less, huh? That's right.
Did you learn Creole and French as a child before you learned English? Oh, yeah. Well, uh, yeah. When I, when I was a kid, I never talked it much.
And actually, we kids didn't talk it much, but, uh, hardly at all. But that's all we listened to. Uh-huh. We, we, huh? Do you remember it?

Oh, I remember quite a, oh, I remember quite a bit of it. Sure. I can understand most of it now. If you talk real slow, you know. We, we had a, we had a dog that, uh, couldn't even understand English.
No kidding. He would, he would bark with a French accent. What would you say to that? That sounds funny, but it's true.
What would you say to that dog, for example, if you wanted to do something?
Well, uh, uh, uh, it's hard for me to remember now. But, uh, what is this name, the dog's name, uh, uh, uh, what is this dog's name?
It wasn't Joseph, because that's my name. Auguste. No, no, it wasn't Auguste. It's Francois. Yeah, that was his name.
That's right, huh?

And, uh, well, not on, not only, uh, the dogs, uh, those French people, like, had chickens and hogs and mules and everything. Like, I used to go out in the country to visit my cousins and things. And, uh, I'd follow them along when some of my cousins in a field plowed, and they would talk to this mule in French, or this horse, or whatever it was plowing, and they understood real good.
I would talk to them in English and nothing would happen.
So, would you describe yourself as a real Creole?
Well, it's, uh, it's different definitions of what a Creole is. Uh, uh, they, they, they claim that a Creole is, uh, French and Spanish.
Uh-huh.
But, uh, the new encyclopedia gives you a little different definition. Yeah.
In Louisiana, uh, any mixture was considered a Creole. Uh-huh.
But you're mainly French, huh? Uh-huh. In all origin.

That's right. Uh, my, uh, in fact, uh, I had a friend of mine, a woman that was kind of a historian, used to come down to the club all the time, and she traced, uh, the name Berensburg, uh, back, uh, and tried to find out exactly what, what, uh, the name intrigued her, you know, Berensburg. Uh-huh. So, she came to the club one night, and she said, man, she says, Joe, she says, she said, I always thought you was a distinguished looking guy. She says, she says, you know, you, you, you've got royal blood in your veins. Is that so? She says, the name Berensburg came from the Count de Berensburg in France. Uh-huh. See? Uh-huh. And she brought a little article in and showed me. And she says, by golly, she says, I'm honored to know you, sir.
I said, how about that? How about that? It made me feel good, you know. Okay.
So, uh, first you studied violin and piano? Yep. You mean seriously?
Well, how, yeah, how, how happened, well, the violin wasn't too serious, because I had a brother taking violin. Yeah.
So, I thought I would, uh, uh, up until, uh, my brother started taking music lessons, I was about ten years old, and my brother hadn't been taking lessons about two years, and, uh,
uh, uh, Papa used to tell me, he says, well, he says, I'm paying a twenty-five cents a lesson. Uh-huh.

For Frank to take lessons, that was my brother, he says, uh, so he says, uh, why don't you sit in there and listen? He says, uh, we can save a little money, maybe. He says, maybe you can learn something, too. Uh-huh. So, that's how I got started, and he got me a little fiddle. Uh-huh. But, uh, I didn't care too much for it. I really liked piano, that's, that's what I liked. Uh-huh. I still like it. Do you still play it a little? No, not too much. Uh-uh.
So, once you started to play clarinet, did, uh, how long before you became a professional musician?
Well, my brother and I started, had a band when I was about, uh, fourteen years old. We used to play parties, and we played. Where did your brother play? Violin.
Was he older than you?

Yeah. Two years older than I am. Uh-huh. And, uh, when I was there, well, I was about, uh, sixteen, when I started, uh, making money. I say, you're a professional when you start making money, aren't you? That's right. Well, I was a pro when I was sixteen, because I was making a little change then, you know, charging two and three dollars for a gig. Could you read music? Oh, yeah. Yeah. When I started playing.
Did most of the guys you played with read music?
All of those guys in Tuts Johnson's band read music. Yeah. Buddy Petey was a good musician. Real good musician.
Would you say as long as that sounds better than you heard?

Yes, sir. Louis says that, too. Uh-huh. Louis and Buddy was good friends. I was talking to Louis about Buddy not too long ago, and he's telling me when Buddy died, he said he buried him. Oh, yeah? He's the one who put up the money for his funeral.
He buried, uh, Joe Oliver, too. Did Louis tell you about Joe before he died? Louis said, Joe, Joe was working. Well, he wasn't working. He had a little fruit stand in Atlanta, Georgia.
Uh-huh.

So, when Louis went to look him up, he went to Atlanta to look him up and said, Joe, Joe was fusing around, was fooling around, straightening up a little counter there. He had some bananas and things on it. Louis said he walked up and he touched Joe on the shoulder. And Joe looked around and he said, well, you son of a bitch.
Louis said he hadn't seen Joe in about, uh, oh, God, 10 or 12 years.
And, uh, I forget when that was. Joe died right after that, too. Louis buried him. Louis's pretty good about things like that, you know.
So, uh, how long did you stay with Tush Johnson?

Oh, I didn't play with Tush Johnson too long, or maybe a year. Those bands didn't work, uh, too regular. Uh-huh. I didn't, I didn't make any out-of-town jobs with them, because, uh, Papa wouldn't let me. You were too young. Yeah. Did they play what out of town?
Yeah.
Like where?
They used to go to New Orleans and play. How far is this from back then?
About 80 miles.
They used to go and play in New Orleans?
But they didn't go with them, huh? No.

I never did make a job in New Orleans, because my father wouldn't let me. Papa wouldn't let me. But they used to go to New Orleans and give all of those bands in New Orleans a fit. And they used to play. I mean really cut them. Really? Yes, sir. This Tush Johnson's band was really a good band. What did Tush Johnson play? Played banjo and guitar.
Uh, I run into a trombone player named Tram, not, uh, when I was up in Seattle. I used to play with that band. Oh, yeah?
Yeah.
But it's funny, uh, uh, uh, you're the one that tell about, bro, about the Creole deal.

Uh, Sonny Greer was telling me this, uh, says, uh, they was playing in, uh, Birmingham, Alabama. And, uh, Sonny says, uh, Sonny says, actually, he says, nobody can tell that I'm, uh, colored, he says, uh. So, Sonny says, he went right downtown and started, and went in, uh, a white restaurant. Sonny Greer did? Yeah, Sonny Greer. When he, when, when, when Bro and them was with Duke, see? Okay. And Sonny says, uh, he was sitting in there, eating, and, uh, he says, Bro happened to pass by. And Bro seen him in there. So, Bro come in there and he says, uh, this counter where he was sitting, uh, he said, had an empty stool and Bro come sit down right next to him. Sonny says, uh, Sonny says, he kind of nudged Bro when he come in there. He says, look, man, he says, be careful. He says, don't talk to me. He says, you know, he says, I'm passing. He says, nobody can tell I'm colored. And he says, but you, he says, I don't know.
And Sonny, you know who could pass the best? Sonny had his hair all gassed and everything. Yeah. Sonny says, man, he says, I was all straight and everything.

He says, Bro sat on there. And he says, man, he says, I was eating a steak there. And he says, Bro sat on there for five minutes and for 10 minutes. And nobody waited on him. So finally Bro called the waitress over and says, uh, Miss, can I get a little service here? And the waitress looked at him and says, uh, says, I'm sorry. She says, but, uh, we don't serve colored people in here. He says, Bro looked at him.
What do you mean you don't serve colored people? He says, I, I will thank you to know that I'm a Creole. His waitress looked at him. He says, uh, I don't give a damn what you are and how old you are.
He says, we do not serve colored people. He says, oh, no. No. No. No. No. So, Joe, uh, what, what do you do after you, after O.C., uh, what's his name? What's his name? What's that, O.T.O.S.?

The Toothjohnker? Toothjohnker. Well, I left, uh, Baton Rouge and went to work, uh, my brother and I got a little job playing a, uh, kind of a Catholic convention in a little town named Opelousa, Louisiana, and we took a band over there, and I went to work with a, a family band. I stayed, uh, a fellow named, uh, Martell's Officer, called Louisiana Ramblers.
They offered me this job, and, uh, I stayed and worked with them.
At this time, you were playing only clarinet, huh? That's right.

And finally, uh, a medicine show came through Opelousa's, Dr. Moon. That's what you hear me talking about all the time. So, Dr. Moon offered me a job. He wanted me to play a saxophone and clarinet. So, Dr. Moon bought me a saxophone. Cause I didn't have no room.
The White Man, Dr. Moon?

Yeah. It's a medicine show. Real, I mean, it was a real fine. Well, in, in those days, uh, you'd compare almost, uh, Dr. Moon's medicine show with that one LeBlanc had. Uh-huh. LeBlanc didn't have nothing but a medicine show, but it was really a big one. But, Dr. Moon had a, had a big special-made bus at that time. Uh, probably cost about, uh, $30,000. Yeah. Yeah. We had those vats on there that we could mix that medicine in.
You mean a bus that, uh, a real, you know, was...

We had, we had real, we had a little room space away on this bus. It was almost the size of a, a railroad car. And the whole company traveled on this one, though? That's right. How many people? Oh, sometimes we had about four or five pieces in the band. But how many other people were connected with the thing? Well, it was Dr. Moon and his wife and the driver.

Of course, in those days, uh, the entertainers had to help with the work, too, you know. I had to help pitch the platform on the lot that you show it on. And the back of this bus, they had a, they had a stage built. Almost like the observation. Now, when did you join? What year was it? This was, uh, 1926.
26. Oh. You were about... The latter part of 25, right? You were about 19, 20 years old.
Yeah. That's right. So anyway, Doc bought me that, uh, at, uh, the saxophone. And, uh,
we started... The first time we played after Hopeloos was Lafayette, Louisiana. That's where, uh, Haddock Hall originated, too. LeBlanc, you know, made Haddock Hall there.

And then, then we went on up north. We played all around the big town. St. Louis. And when I got to St. Louis on the medicine show, that's the first time that I run into, uh, Charlie Crest and Faith Merrill. Uh-huh.
Well, Faith Merrill was, was he playing on the boat? That's right.
Faith was, Faith was mostly playing on the boat, and Charlie Crest had the, this, uh, plantation. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Market Street there.
Uh-huh. Tell us a little about Dr. Moon's operation, right? Uh-huh. Did you say they had a platform on the back of the bus?
They had a, uh, uh, uh, kind of a stage built. Something similar to an observation platform, you know, in the back of the...
Suppose, suppose you arrive in a small town. Just tell us all the things you have to do. Suppose you drive into a place.
When we drove into a place, Doc went ahead in advance, and he got the, uh, the setup for the lot that we was going to play on, and the license here to have a license.

To play this, huh? All right, we drove, uh, we had the option to sleep on the bus if we wanted to, because he had little bunks on this bus. Uh, something similar to a brace on all over there. A car. Uh-huh. Or else we could get a room if we wanted, because medicine shows played from a week to two weeks.
Oh, you said in the town?
Oh, yeah.

Most of it, mostly just a week. Uh-huh. Sometimes two weeks, though, business was real good. Uh-huh. But when we got to a town, we went directly to the, this empty lot that we was going to play. We had a portable platform that you assemble.
Uh-huh.
With a curtain, and, uh, these, these old-time, uh, carbon lights, or gas lights, or whatever you call them. We set the platform up, and we got that up.
On the back of the bus, or just, just a platform?

No, the platform was set up separate, in the lot, in the field. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. If it was any grass to be cut, we had to cut that. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. All that sort of stuff. After we set the platform up, we got our costumes on. What kind of costume did you wear?

Uh-huh. I had a clown costume to start off with. Uh-huh. Because I, uh, I was the kind of imitating, I got the idea from the Six Brown Brothers. You remember the old Six Brown Brothers? Yeah. Used to wear clown costumes, playing saxophone. They had a saxophone sextet they did. Yeah. Uh, that was one of my uniforms. That was starting. Then I used to sing romantic songs, you know. I had a fair voice too. You mean straight or?

Straight. Let me call you Sweetheart and Mahajie, man. I'd take off good on those numbers. Yeah? What did the other guys, what kind of a guy did you have? We had comedians, we, well it was a variety show. And how many musicians in there? Uh, that, uh, about four or five, all of you, we never had no straight comedians. Uh-huh. Everybody was doubling. Everybody had a doubling. Musicians had a double. What instruments? Them cats had to do everything.
What instruments? What instruments?
This show had, uh, when I joined Dr. Moon, they had a violin player, had a banjo player, had a clarinet player, and they had a guitar player.
Uh-huh. That was a combination. Uh-huh. And two of them was comedians in this bunch. I see.
So, uh, getting back to what we did when we get to the town. Uh-huh. After, after we set up the platform and got that straightened out, we would get on the back of this bus.

Uh-huh. Doc, this Doc Moon was a kind of versatile guy. How old was he at that time? Who, Doc Moon? Yeah. Oh, he wasn't old at that time. Uh, Doc was about, uh, oh, I imagine about 35 years old. What did he look like?

He was a little bit of short guy. He was almost a midget. He was a little less than five feet tall. Thin? No. Very muscular. Very muscular. Very muscular. In fact, uh, he, he, uh, the part of the show, he used to do, uh, tricks. He had a rigging that they set up too on the platform. Tricks on the barbell, you know. He was an acrobat, huh?
That's right. That's the, that's the thing I wanted to get out. He was an acrobat. And a darn good one. Oh, yeah? Yeah.

The funny thing about Doc Moon, the guy had a lot of money. He did? But, uh, he never paid for a haircut. Uh, during those days of Mola Barber College used to give free haircuts. Ha! Ha! Ha! Doc would wait, wait until we got to a big town like St. Louis around Chicago. We played, we never played directly in the big towns. We played outskirts like Gary, Indiana. Yes. Doc would wait until he got there, and I'm going to go over the Barber College and go get a haircut. Ha! And some of them haircuts was really something to see, man. Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! That always stuck to me as a funny thing, this cat with all that money. Ha! Ha! Ha! Looked like somebody had cut it with a knife. Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha!

pages.label: 002_Joe Darensbourg and Minor "Ram" Hall Interview, 1957-04-18 Part 2

blocks.x: Joe Derensburg, April 18, 1957, Real 2.
So anyway, that was a part of the show. I used to like to see him do those things. He'd get on those rings and things like that, and he had some bars.
Was it all on this platform? All on this platform. It was a big platform.
Well, the platform was fully as big as this room.

Yeah, and then you'd have all these things assembled on this platform. That's right. That's right. And you had set up the instrument. That's right. And then, so start. Now what happened? How'd you get the people in there? What'd you do?
We would ballyhoo through town. When we got to town, Doc would have a banner.

The top part was Doc Moon's medicine show, famous entertainers and different things like that. And showing at 346 Mott Street or some street like that, that's starting at 8 o'clock. Well, people was used to that kind of stuff in those days, and they would wait for it. You know, they never heard anything. You know, they didn't get too much entertainment. No radio or television in those days.
But we would play on the street corners, something similar to the way the bands used to ballyhoo and Baton Rouge advertising their dances.

Uh-huh. And people used to just lay for those medicine shows, because that was a regular occurrence. And when, when, when that, oh, about 6 o'clock people would start congregating around that platform, waiting for the show. See? When did the show start?
About 8 o'clock. It would last from about 8 to 9.30. Uh-huh. Hour and a half show usually.
And what, what else was on the show?
Well, Doc, Doc Moon would open the show with a,

he would come out there and he says, uh, look, he says, folks, I don't think you would say good evening. He's very informal, you know. He says, uh, I want you to know right now, he says, uh, that I'm not out here to make money. I didn't, uh, organize this show to make money, to get all these great entertainers together. And then look over at us, you know, man.
He says, why, these boys here could be playing in Carnegie Hall in New York and different places. In fact, I got some of them from,
uh, Carnegie Hall or something. He had some high-powered speech, he would tell there.
And he says, if, uh, if you think that I'm out here having this show to make money, he says,

I want you to leave right now. He says, to show you, I don't want to make any money off of this deal. Then he had a, he'd have about five dollars worth of change in his hand, you see, some half of dollars and some quarters and nickels and dimes and pennies. They had a lot of pennies, you know, man, who would rattle like hell. He'd stick his hand in the sack and pull it out there. And he says, to show you, I don't need any money,

he says, here, and throw it out in the audience. Man, it was a scramble. Them cats were killing themselves picking up that money, you know, it looked like a hundred dollars then. A lot of times I'd jump off the stand and pick up a quarter myself and get on the side there.
No kidding.
So, well, well, well, right there, the psychology of the thing got the guys, you know. And then,
after that, he wouldn't press them then, you know, about the medicine.
Uh,
what was the medicine?
What was it called? Moon tonic. Moon tonic. Moonshine.
Moon tonic. Well, it was, well, you could say moonshine, all right, and you'd be pretty close to it.
But I, this, this is, this is some real great medicine. Uh, after I was with the show about six or seven weeks, I worked up to what you would more or less say as a head came in.
